"Busts 4 Justice remain committed to making things better for busty women on the high street, but for now we're happy just to be able to encourage all ladies to reward themselves and their boobs with some properly fitted, fairly priced lingerie." "They may get cleared out by the time the weekend is over!"

# Marks & Spencer Scraps Extra Fees for Larger Bra Sizes After Public Backlash

**LONDON, England (CNN)** -- British department store Marks & Spencer admitted on Friday that its practice of charging more for larger bras had been a mistake, announcing plans to eliminate the pricing disparity for its bigger lingerie items.

The retailer's apology appeared in a striking full-page newspaper advertisement across Britain, headlined with a punny confession: "We boobed."

Facing mounting pressure from consumer advocates, the company backed down from its policy of tacking on an extra £2 ($3) charge for bras sized DD and above. According to the advertisement, "It's true that our fantastic quality larger bras cost more money to make, and we felt it was right to reflect this in the prices we charged. Well, we were wrong."

This reversal comes after nearly twelve months of pressure from an online movement called Busts 4 Justice, organized through Facebook. The group's founders contended that since competing retailers didn't impose similar surcharges, Marks & Spencer had no justification for doing so either—especially given that the chain already sold larger clothing sizes without any markup, making the bra pricing policy inconsistent.

Group administrators Becky Mount and Beckie Williams celebrated the victory in a Facebook post Friday, expressing gratitude to supporters: "We would like to thank everyone who has supported us on this issue; especially the thousands of brilliant, busty women that have joined forces with us. We couldn't have done this without you." They added that while their campaign for fair treatment of well-endowed women would continue, they were pleased to encourage shoppers to invest in "properly fitted, fairly priced lingerie."

As a beloved British institution, Marks & Spencer has built its reputation on dependable, affordably-priced essentials, with its lingerie section serving as a go-to destination for shoppers nationwide—particularly renowned for solid, no-frills basics.

Sweetening the deal further, the retailer also revealed a temporary 25 percent discount on all bras throughout the remainder of May.

Mount acknowledged the goodwill gesture in her post: "I think even though we all obviously held a bit of a grudge against buying our bras from M&S we should really be grateful they got rid of the surcharge and have given us the super generous 25 percent off. They may get cleared out by the time the weekend is over!"

# Marks & Spencer Ends Controversial Bra Pricing Policy

Marks & Spencer, one of Britain's most well-known retailers, has issued a public apology for a pricing practice that many customers had long considered discriminatory: charging more for bras in larger sizes. The company announced it would eliminate this surcharge, marking a significant reversal after months of mounting criticism.

## The Surcharge in Question

For years, Marks & Spencer had added an extra charge of up to £2 (approximately $3) to bras in sizes DD and above. When questioned about this practice, the company defended the pricing structure by pointing to the higher manufacturing costs associated with producing bras with additional support, more fabric, and reinforced construction needed for larger sizes.

## A Grassroots Campaign for Change

The turning point came through the efforts of a determined group of consumers who organized under the banner Busts 4 Justice, a Facebook group that spearheaded a campaign lasting nearly a full year. Led by campaigners Becky Mount and Beckie Williams, the group systematically challenged Marks & Spencer's justification for the pricing disparity, keeping pressure on the retailer through sustained public advocacy and social media engagement.

## The Core of the Argument

Central to the campaigners' case was a simple but compelling point of comparison: neither Marks & Spencer nor its competitors charged extra for larger sizes in other clothing categories. Whether shopping for trousers, dresses, or shirts, customers paid the same price regardless of size. Campaigners argued that singling out bras for size-based surcharges was inconsistent and unfairly penalized women with larger busts, who already often face limited options and higher costs when shopping for well-fitting undergarments.

## The Outcome

Bowing to sustained public pressure, Marks & Spencer not only agreed to scrap the surcharge entirely but went a step further by announcing a 25 percent price reduction across its entire bra range. This move was seen as a substantial win for consumer advocacy, demonstrating how organized grassroots campaigns can successfully influence corporate pricing policies. The decision was welcomed by customers and equality advocates alike, who viewed it as a step toward more equitable pricing practices in the retail industry.

# Marks & Spencer Ends Controversial "Fat Tax" on Larger Bra Sizes

Marks & Spencer, one of Britain's most iconic and trusted retail institutions, has officially discontinued its long-standing practice of charging women more for bras in larger cup sizes, following sustained pressure from a passionate consumer advocacy campaign that captured national attention over the better part of a year.

## The Campaign That Started It All

The controversy centered on a Facebook group called Busts 4 Justice, which was formed by frustrated customers who noticed a troubling pattern: bras in DD cup sizes and above consistently carried a price premium of up to £2 more than their smaller-sized counterparts. What began as a grassroots complaint quickly gathered momentum as members of the group pointed out the inherent unfairness of this pricing structure.

Their argument was straightforward yet compelling: this was not standard industry practice, nor was it consistent with M&S's own broader business model. Other clothing retailers across the market did not impose similar surcharges based on bra size, and perhaps more damning was the fact that M&S's own clothing lines—from dresses to trousers to outerwear—did not penalize customers for purchasing larger sizes. Critics argued that singling out bras for this kind of size-based pricing discrimination was both illogical and discriminatory, effectively punishing women for having larger busts.

## Nearly a Year of Sustained Pressure

For close to twelve months, the Busts 4 Justice campaign kept the issue in the public eye, organizing supporters, raising awareness, and applying consistent pressure on M&S to reconsider its pricing policy. The campaign resonated with many consumers who felt that such pricing practices reflected a broader pattern of companies imposing hidden costs on larger-sized shoppers, sometimes referred to informally as a "fat tax."

## M&S Responds: Apology and Price Cuts

Faced with mounting public criticism and the reputational risk of appearing tone-deaf to consumer concerns, Marks & Spencer ultimately relented. The company not only agreed to eliminate the size-based surcharge but did so with a notably self-deprecating and high-profile public apology, launching an advertising campaign built around the punny slogan "We boobed"—a lighthearted yet clear acknowledgment that the company had made a mistake.

Going beyond simply correcting the original issue, M&S sweetened the resolution by announcing an across-the-board price reduction of 25% on all bras sold in their stores, regardless of size. This broader price cut was seen as an effort to rebuild goodwill with customers and demonstrate genuine commitment to fair pricing practices, rather than simply making the minimum concession necessary to quiet critics.

## A Broader Victory for Consumer Advocacy

The resolution of this campaign has been widely celebrated as a meaningful victory for consumer advocacy movements, particularly those focused on challenging size-based discrimination in retail pricing. It serves as a notable example of how organized, sustained public pressure—even when originating from a relatively informal social media group—can successfully compel major corporations to reconsider and reform their business practices. For many observers, the outcome represents not just a win on the specific issue of bra pricing, but a broader statement about the power of consumer voices in holding retailers accountable for practices perceived as unfair or discriminatory based on body size.

Marks & Spencer, one of Britain's most iconic retailers, has scrapped its long-standing policy of charging more for bras in larger sizes, following sustained pressure from customers and campaigners who labeled the practice discriminatory.

## The Policy That Sparked Outrage

For years, M&S customers requiring larger cup sizes or wider back bands paid a premium of up to £4 more than those buying standard sizes. Critics argued this amounted to a "tax" on women whose bodies didn't fit conventional sizing—effectively penalizing them for something entirely outside their control.

The pricing structure meant that women needing DD cups or larger, or those with wider frames, were consistently paying more for basic, everyday garments than their smaller-chested counterparts, despite the products often using similar amounts of material and manufacturing processes.

## Campaigners Push Back

The campaign against what activists dubbed the "boob tax" gained significant momentum on social media, where women shared receipts and screenshots highlighting the price discrepancies.

"This isn't about asking for special treatment," said one campaign organizer. "It's about basic fairness. Why should someone be charged more simply because their body doesn't conform to a 'standard' size? We don't see this kind of surcharge applied to men's clothing in nearly the same way."

Another organizer emphasized the broader implications: "This policy disproportionately affected women who already struggle to find well-fitting, affordable underwear. Larger-chested women often report spending more time and money just trying to find bras that fit properly and offer adequate support. Adding a financial penalty on top of that felt like insult added to injury."

Petitions calling for retailers to abandon size-based pricing collected thousands of signatures, with organizers pointing to research suggesting the average bra size in the UK has increased in recent decades—meaning more women than ever were affected by the surcharge.

## M&S Responds

Facing mounting public pressure and negative press coverage, M&S announced it would standardize pricing across its bra range, regardless of size. In a statement, the company acknowledged customer feedback and emphasized its commitment to inclusivity.

"We've listened carefully to our customers," an M&S spokesperson said. "We want all women to feel valued and supported when shopping with us, and that includes ensuring our pricing reflects fairness across our entire size range."

## A Broader Industry Reckoning

M&S's decision places pressure on competitors who maintain similar size-based pricing structures. Campaigners hope this move will trigger industry-wide change, forcing other major retailers to reassess their own policies.

"This is a significant win, but it's just the beginning," said one activist involved in the campaign. "We're calling on other retailers to follow M&S's lead immediately. No woman should have to pay more for a bra simply because of her size."

Consumer rights advocates have framed the decision as part of a larger conversation about "pink tax" pricing—where products marketed to women often cost more than comparable men's products—and hope it signals growing corporate accountability on gender-based pricing disparities.

For many customers, the change represents more than just pounds and pence saved. It's an acknowledgment that body diversity shouldn't come with a financial penalty.
